lessons.unit: Spec 1.5: The Sunnah of the Prophet (Section A)
lessons.title: 1.5 The Sunnah: what it is and why it matters (Qur'an 33:36)
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do Muslims treat the Prophet's words and actions as a guide for life?
objectives: Define Sunnah and hadith and the three forms of Sunnah
Explain why the Sunnah matters to Muslims
Analyse Qur'an 33:36 and link it to obedience
successCriteria: All: define Sunnah and give an example of a saying, an action and an approval
Most: explain two reasons the Sunnah is important, with a Qur'an reference
Some: evaluate how far Muslims could practise Islam without the Sunnah
lessons.crossCurricular: English: distinguishing a source from a summary; History: types of source
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: love and obedience expressed through following the example of the Messenger

keywords.def: the way of the Prophet: his sayings, deeds and approvals
a report that records what the Prophet said, did or approved

starter: Bismillah. Name the five pillars of Islam.
Which pillar is Salah, and how many times a day is it performed?
Who compiled the Qur'an into one volume under Abu Bakr?

teach.heading: What is the Sunnah?
bullets: Sunnah: the Prophet's way of life
Three forms: saying (qawl), action (fi'l), approval (taqrir)
Hadith: the report that carries the Sunnah
Qur'an is revelation; Sunnah explains and applies it
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Ask pupils for one thing the Prophet ﷺ did that they copy (for example, saying bismillah before food). Sort their answers into saying, action, approval. Make clear that hadith is the report and Sunnah is the practice reported. Note for the teacher: Muslim scholars use 'Sunnah' in several senses (for example, in fiqh it can also mean a recommended act). Here it means his whole way as the spec requires.

teach.heading: Three forms of Sunnah
bullets: Saying: a spoken teaching
Action: what he was seen doing
Approval: he saw something and did not object
teach.note: Give one example of each without needing a reference: a saying (teaching about good character), an action (how he prayed), an approval (Companions doing something in his presence and him allowing it). If the teacher wants a numbered hadith to quote, supply and verify it before the lesson; the three categories are the point.

teach.heading: Why does it matter? Qur'an 33:36
bullets: Qur'an 33:36: when Allah ﷻ and His Messenger decide a matter, believers have no choice
Qur'an 33:21: the Messenger is a beautiful example
Qur'an 4:80: obeying the Messenger is obeying Allah ﷻ
Qur'an 59:7: take what the Messenger gives
teach.note: 33:36 is the set passage (spec 1.5). Ayat references here are ones the school can rely on: 33:36, 33:21, 4:80, 59:7. Read 33:36 slowly in Arabic then English: وَمَا كَانَ لِمُؤْمِنٍ وَلَا مُؤْمِنَةٍ إِذَا قَضَى اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ أَمْرًا أَن يَكُونَ لَهُمُ الْخِيَرَةُ مِنْ أَمْرِهِمْ. Ask: what does 'no choice' mean? (No believer may set aside a ruling once clear; not that people cannot ask questions.) Teacher to check the Arabic text against a mushaf before display. Historical context: scholars mention an occasion about a marriage proposal arranged by the Prophet ﷺ; if used, give the source.

teach.heading: Model answer: explain why the Sunnah matters
bullets: Claim, reason, evidence
Link back to the question
teach.note: Model how to write a 6-mark 'explain' answer using PEEL: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link.

model.problem: Explain two reasons why the Sunnah is important to Muslims. (6 marks)
steps: Reason 1: it shows how to follow the Qur'an in practice, for example the Qur'an commands prayer but the Prophet ﷺ showed how to perform it.
Evidence: Qur'an 33:21 calls him a beautiful example, so Muslims copy his actions.
Reason 2: it is a source of authority; Qur'an 4:80 says obeying the Messenger is obeying Allah ﷻ.
Link: so a Muslim cannot practise Islam fully without learning and following the Sunnah.
model.answer: Full marks need two developed reasons, each with a reference or example and an explanation of why it matters.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Choose the best answer on whiteboards
teach.note: Show the check; cold-call two pupils to justify, then reveal.

check.q: A Companion saw the Prophet ﷺ pray and prayed the same way. Which form of Sunnah did the Prophet's way of praying belong to?
check.why: Fi'l: it is something he did. Qawl is something he said; taqrir is silent approval of someone else's act; the Qur'an is revelation recited, not the Sunnah.

practice: Give one example each of qawl, fi'l and taqrir (teacher supplies prompts).
Identify the phrase in 33:36 that tells believers they do not have a choice.
Explain in two sentences the difference between Sunnah and hadith.
independent: Core: complete the sorting table of ten statements into qawl, fi'l and taqrir.
Extend: write a 6-mark answer 'Explain two reasons why the Sunnah matters to Muslims.'
Stretch: 'Muslims could follow the Qur'an without the Sunnah.' Write the opening of a 12-mark response with a counter-view.
exit: Define hadith in one sentence.
Name two Qur'an references that support following the Prophet ﷺ.
Big question: why do Muslims treat the Prophet's words and actions as a guide?
lessons.homework: Learn the definitions of Sunnah, hadith, qawl, fi'l and taqrir and write one example of each.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sentence starters and a pre-sorted example bank; stretch: compare how Sunnah is described in the main Muslim traditions (Sunni and Shia both follow the Prophet's Sunnah, differing in which chains of narrators they accept).

lessons.unit: Spec 1.5: The Sunnah of the Prophet (Section A)
lessons.title: 1.5 How the Sunnah was recorded and its role in belief and practice
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we know that a hadith really goes back to the Prophet ﷺ?
objectives: Describe how the Sunnah was memorised, written and collected
Explain isnad, matn and the grades of hadith
Explain the role of the Sunnah in establishing belief and practice
successCriteria: All: describe two ways the Sunnah was preserved
Most: explain isnad and how scholars tested a hadith
Some: assess whether the Sunnah is as reliable as the Qur'an, using the spec's key ideas
lessons.crossCurricular: History: evaluating chains of source evidence; English: reliability and bias
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty and trustworthiness (amanah) as the basis of knowledge

keywords.def: the chain of narrators of a hadith
authentic: reliable narrators and sound chain
one of the most trusted hadith collections, compiled by Imam al-Bukhari

starter: Name the three forms of Sunnah.
Which Qur'an passage says believers have no choice once Allah ﷻ and His Messenger decide?

teach.heading: Preserving the Sunnah
bullets: Memory: Companions learned and repeated what they heard
Practice: the community prayed, fasted and performed Hajj as he did
Writing: some Companions kept written notes
Collection: scholars gathered hadith in books
teach.note: Stress that the Companions learned the Sunnah in lifetime and lived it. For writing, name Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As (known to have kept a written collection) and the Prophet's permission to write for Abu Shah after the Makkah conquest (Bukhari 2434 is the reference; teacher to verify the number before displaying). Explain that early on the Prophet ﷺ told people to write only the Qur'an so it would not be mixed (a report in Muslim); later writing was allowed. Do not worry if pupils find this a puzzle: scholars explain it by the stage of revelation.

teach.heading: Isnad and matn
bullets: Isnad: who told whom, back to the Prophet ﷺ
Matn: the words of the report
Scholars checked memory, honesty and whether narrators could have met
Grades: sahih, hasan, da'if
teach.note: Draw a chain on the board: Prophet, Companion, Successor, collector. Ask: why would a chain matter? (It shows the source.) Explain that early scholars also checked that the text did not contradict the Qur'an or established facts. Mention the warning against lying about the Prophet ﷺ: 'Whoever lies about me on purpose, let him take his seat in the Fire' (Bukhari 1291 and Muslim 4); teacher to verify before quoting. This explains why scholars were so careful.
cycle: Collector records it with the isnad

teach.heading: The great collections
bullets: Imam al-Bukhari (died 256 AH) and Imam Muslim (died 261 AH)
Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah
Together: the six main Sunni collections
Shia scholars also collect hadith, including from the Imams of the Prophet's family
teach.note: Keep neutral and factual. The Sunni six are called al-Kutub al-Sittah; Bukhari and Muslim are called the two Sahihs. Shia Muslims use their own major collections (for example, al-Kafi) and also revere the Prophet's Sunnah; difference lies in which narrators and chains are accepted. Say this plainly and without ranking.

teach.heading: Role of the Sunnah
bullets: Explains the Qur'an: how to pray, how to perform Hajj
Gives details: amounts and conditions of zakah
Shows how to live Islam as a person, parent and leader
Qur'an 16:44: the Messenger was sent to explain
teach.note: Model the argument: Qur'an says establish prayer; the Sunnah shows the how. Qur'an 16:44 states the Messenger explains what was sent down. Hadith 'Pray as you have seen me pray' (Bukhari 631) is a good link; verify before quoting. Ask: what would Hajj look like with no Sunnah?

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Whiteboards up
teach.note: Reveal after discussion of the distractors.

check.q: What does the isnad of a hadith tell you?
options: The meaning of the hadith in modern English
The chain of people who passed it on
The book of the Qur'an it explains
check.why: The isnad is the chain of narrators. The matn is the text. The other options are not what an isnad shows.

teach.heading: Model answer: 'describe'
bullets: Name the point
Develop with detail
Use correct terms
teach.note: 'Describe' means state the features and develop each. Model with the example below.

model.problem: Describe how the Sunnah was recorded. (4 marks)
steps: Point: it was first memorised by the Companions, who also practised it.
Detail: some Companions wrote hadith down, for example in personal notebooks.
Detail: later scholars collected hadith with isnads into books, such as Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim.
Use terms: scholars graded hadith by the reliability of the narrators in the isnad.
model.answer: Four marks: four distinct, developed points with accurate terms.

practice: Say what isnad means and draw a three-person chain.
Name two of the six collections.
Why did scholars check the narrators?
independent: Core: complete a timeline from the Prophet's lifetime to Imam al-Bukhari.
Extend: write a 'describe' answer on how the Sunnah was recorded (4 marks).
Stretch: 'The Sunnah is as important as the Qur'an.' Write a balanced paragraph using 4:80 and 16:44.
exit: Give one reason scholars graded hadith.
Name the part of a hadith that is the text.
Big question: how do we know a hadith goes back to the Prophet ﷺ?
lessons.homework: Revise: write a 6-mark answer 'Explain the role of the Sunnah in establishing Islamic belief and practice.'
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: chain-of-people diagram, key-word bank; stretch: research the differences in grading between sahih and hasan hadith.

lessons.unit: Spec 1.6: Teachings and example of the Prophet on justice and equality (Section A)
lessons.title: 1.6 Social and economic justice in the Prophet's teaching and example
lessons.bigQuestion: What does it mean to be just in society, and how did the Prophet ﷺ live it?
objectives: Define 'adl and explain Islamic teaching on social and economic justice
Describe the Prophet's example on fairness, wealth and the vulnerable
Analyse the hadith on justice and equality before the law
successCriteria: All: define 'adl and give an example of fair treatment
Most: explain how zakah and fair trade promote economic justice
Some: assess whether the Prophet's example applies to modern society
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: fairness and the rule of law; Citizenship: equality before the law
lessons.smsc: Moral: justice, honesty and care for the vulnerable; Social: responsibility for the community

keywords.def: obligatory giving to those in need

starter: Which pillar of Islam concerns giving to the poor?
Name one thing the Prophet ﷺ did in Madinah to unite the community.
What does 'Seal of the Prophets' mean?

teach.heading: What is justice?
bullets: 'Adl: giving every person what is due
Qur'an 4:135: stand firm for justice, even against yourselves
Qur'an 16:90: Allah ﷻ commands justice and kindness
Justice is part of why messengers were sent (Qur'an 57:25)
teach.note: Open with bismillah. Ask: is fairness the same as treating everyone identically? Explain 'adl as giving each person their right. The ayat 4:135, 16:90 and 57:25 are secure references; teacher to check them against a mushaf before display. Note 5:8 as well: justice even towards those you dislike.

teach.heading: Equality before the law
bullets: A noble woman of Makhzum was caught stealing
Some asked the Prophet ﷺ to spare her
He said: nations before you were destroyed for punishing the weak and sparing the powerful
He said the same law applied even to his own daughter
teach.note: This is a strong candidate for the spec's 'hadith on justice' (Bukhari 3475, Muslim 1688; teacher to verify the number and the exact wording and read it from a trusted translation). Because the spec lists the passage by reference only, check the printed Appendix 5 passage with the pupils. Annotate: who is protected, who is warned, what principle is established. Ask: does rank give immunity? (No.) Link to the rule of law in Britain.

quote.text: The people before you were destroyed because when a noble stole they left him, but when a weak person stole they applied the punishment.
quote.source: Paraphrase of the hadith of the Makhzumi woman: Bukhari 3475, Muslim 1688 (teacher to verify wording)

teach.heading: Economic justice
bullets: Qur'an 59:7: wealth must not circulate only among the rich
Zakah purifies wealth and supports the poor
Riba (interest) is forbidden (Qur'an 2:275)
The Prophet urged fair trade and honest weights
teach.note: Link with 3.4 (Zakah). Teach the principle: wealth is a trust from Allah ﷻ, with duties attached. For fair trade, describe honest measure and avoiding fraud (Qur'an 83:1-3 on those who give short measure is secure; teacher to verify). The Prophet's own trade with Khadijah was known for honesty (Unit 1.1). Ask pupils to give one modern example of unfair economic practice.

teach.heading: Care for the weak
bullets: Orphans: Qur'an 93:9 do not oppress the orphan
Workers: they are your brothers (Bukhari 30, Muslim 1661)
The Prophet warned against oppression on the Day of Judgment (Muslim 2578)
Freed slaves were honoured, for example Bilal
teach.note: Teacher to verify the hadith numbers (Bukhari 30 on treating servants as brothers; Muslim 2578 on oppression being darkness on the Day of Resurrection). If not able to check, teach the ideas without numbers. Explain the context: slavery existed worldwide; Islam encouraged freeing slaves and demanded humane treatment. Do not over-claim. Ask: how does this show Muslim beliefs about society?

teach.heading: Model answer
bullets: Use the passage
Name the principle
Explain the link to society
teach.note: Model a 6-mark answer with evidence.

model.problem: Explain how the Prophet's teaching and example promoted justice. (6 marks)
steps: Point 1: he applied the same law to everyone, shown when he refused to excuse a noble thief because of rank.
Explain: this teaches that no one is above the law, which creates fairness in society.
Point 2: he taught that wealth must reach the poor, through zakah and the ban on riba.
Explain: this reduces poverty and shows Muslims they are responsible for each other.
Link: so Muslim society is meant to be one of accountability and care.
model.answer: Both points developed with an example and an explanation.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Reveal and discuss.

check.q: What does the hadith about the woman of Makhzum teach?
options: Rich people may be forgiven for crimes
Punishment applies equally to everyone, whatever their rank
Stealing is only wrong in Makkah
check.why: The Prophet applied the law equally. The other options reverse the principle of equality before the law.

practice: Define 'adl in your own words.
Identify one economic teaching and its source.
Why did the Prophet ﷺ refuse to excuse the noble thief?
independent: Core: complete a table: situation, injustice, what the Prophet ﷺ taught.
Extend: write a 6-mark answer on economic justice in Islam.
Stretch: write 8 lines on whether the Prophet's rule of equality applies in a British court.
exit: Give two Islamic sources on justice.
Define zulm.
Big question: what does it mean to be just in society?
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph: 'The Prophet's example shows that justice is more than punishment.' Support it with two pieces of evidence.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: visual story map of the Makhzumi woman event; stretch: compare Islamic and British ideas of equality before the law.

lessons.unit: Spec 1.6: Teachings and example of the Prophet on justice and equality (Section A)
lessons.title: 1.6 Human rights and relations with people of other religions
lessons.bigQuestion: How should Muslims treat people whose beliefs differ from theirs?
objectives: Describe the Prophet's teaching and example on human rights
Describe his relationships with people of other religions
Explain what this shows about Muslim beliefs about society
successCriteria: All: name two rights the Prophet ﷺ protected
Most: explain his relations with Jews, Christians and others with examples
Some: assess how far the Prophet's example supports religious tolerance today
lessons.crossCurricular: Citizenship: human rights, freedom of belief; History: treaties and covenants
lessons.smsc: Social: living respectfully in a diverse society; Cultural: understanding religious diversity

keywords.def: non-Muslim citizens under Muslim protection (term used in early Muslim states)
covenant or constitution: the Madinah agreement

starter: Give one example of economic justice in Islam.
Name the hadith topic you annotated last lesson.

teach.heading: Rights in the Farewell Sermon
bullets: Life, property and honour of every Muslim are sacred
The Prophet declared these rights in the sermon at Arafah
Qur'an 17:70: Allah ﷻ has honoured the children of Adam
Qur'an 5:32: killing one innocent life is like killing all
teach.note: The sacredness of life, wealth and honour is in the Farewell Sermon (Bukhari 1739 and others; verify). Say clearly that 17:70 and 5:32 apply to people as people. Ask: what rights does the sermon protect? Tie to the modern idea of human rights while noting that the Islamic basis is the dignity given by Allah ﷻ. Avoid using this as a debate about modern charters; the spec asks about the Prophet's teaching.

teach.heading: The covenant of Madinah
bullets: After the Hijrah the Prophet ﷺ agreed a pact with Madinah's tribes
Muslims, Jews and others formed one political community
Each group kept its own religion
All would defend Madinah if attacked
teach.note: This is the document known as the Sahifah or Constitution of Madinah, recorded in the early Sira (Ibn Ishaq). Present as a historical agreement; scholars discuss details and wording, so keep to well-known points: religious freedom and mutual defence. Note for the teacher: a later breakdown with some tribes was about treason and breaking the agreement, not about faith (see Spec 1.7).

head: Group
Rights under the covenant
rows: One community with duties of defence
Freedom of religion, allies in defence

teach.heading: Other faiths in his example
bullets: No compulsion in religion (Qur'an 2:256)
Qur'an 109:6: you have your religion and I have mine
Kindness to peaceful non-Muslims (Qur'an 60:8)
He stood when a Jewish funeral passed (Bukhari 1312)
teach.note: The ayah references are secure; verify 1312 and Muslim's parallel before quoting. Also describe the Christian delegation of Najran being received in Madinah (Sira). A well-known hadith warns against wronging a non-Muslim under covenant (Bukhari 3166); verify before displaying. Make clear: Muslims believe Islam is true but do not force belief.

teach.heading: Model answer
bullets: Evidence
Explanation
Wider belief
teach.note: Model an 'Explain' answer.

model.problem: Explain how the Prophet's treatment of people of other religions shows Muslim beliefs about society. (6 marks)
steps: Point: he agreed the Madinah covenant, giving Jews and others freedom to follow their religion.
Explain: this shows Muslims believe a society can include different faiths under shared rules.
Point: he stood for the funeral of a Jewish man, which shows respect for human life and dignity.
Explain: this shows Muslim belief that all people deserve respect because Allah ﷻ honoured human beings.
model.answer: Two points, each with evidence and explanation linked to belief about society.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Discuss before revealing.

check.q: Which statement best describes the Madinah covenant?
options: It forced everyone to become Muslim
It set up a shared community where groups kept their religion and defended the city together
check.why: The covenant protected religious freedom and agreed shared defence; compulsion is rejected by 2:256.

practice: Name two rights protected in the Farewell Sermon.
Which ayah says there is no compulsion in religion?
What was the covenant of Madinah?
independent: Core: write one sentence for each: life, property, honour, religious freedom.
Extend: write a 6-mark answer on his relationships with people of other religions.
Stretch: write 8 lines on whether the covenant of Madinah can inform life in modern Britain.
exit: Give one example of kindness to a non-Muslim.
Define huquq.
Big question: how should Muslims treat people whose beliefs differ?
lessons.homework: Prepare a 2-minute talk: 'Islam and respect for others'. Use two sources.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sentence starters and a visual of the covenant; stretch: contrast the Madinah covenant with the Magna Carta as agreements about rights.

lessons.unit: Spec 1.6: Teachings and example of the Prophet on justice and equality (Section A)
lessons.title: 1.6 Respect for mothers and women, and what the teachings show about Muslim society
lessons.bigQuestion: What do the Prophet's teachings on mothers and women show about the kind of society Muslims aim to build?
objectives: Describe the Prophet's teaching and example on respect for mothers
Describe his teaching and example on respect for women
Evaluate what these teachings show about Muslim beliefs about society
successCriteria: All: say how the Prophet ﷺ taught Muslims to treat mothers
Most: explain two examples of his treatment of women
Some: evaluate a claim that Islam values women, with a balanced judgement
lessons.crossCurricular: Citizenship: equality and rights; PSHE: respect in relationships
lessons.smsc: Moral: kindness and respect; Social: the family as the basis of society

keywords.def: Mothers of the Believers: the Prophet's wives
the gift the husband gives the wife at marriage

starter: Which hadith did we use for equality before the law?
Give one right protected in the Farewell Sermon.

teach.heading: Mothers: the greatest claim
bullets: A man asked who deserved his best company
The Prophet said: your mother, three times, then your father
Qur'an 31:14 and 46:15 speak of the mother's hardship
Kindness to parents is ranked next to worship of Allah ﷻ (Qur'an 17:23)
teach.note: Hadith: Bukhari 5971 and Muslim 2548 (Abu Hurayra); verify the wording before display. Ask: why does the mother come three times? (Pregnancy, childbirth, nursing; scholars comment on it.) Be sensitive to pupils whose mothers are absent or who live in hard circumstances; speak of the duty as kindness within what is possible. 46:15-18 is also the set passage in unit 3.8, so this can return then.

quote.text: Your mother, then your mother, then your mother, then your father.
quote.source: Hadith on best companionship: Bukhari 5971, Muslim 2548 (verify wording)

teach.heading: Women in the Prophet's example
bullets: Qur'an 33:35: believing men and women share the same promised reward
Qur'an 4:19: live with wives in kindness
He listened to the advice of Umm Salamah at Hudaybiyyah
He helped at home and treated his family gently
teach.note: Teach accurately: spiritual equality of men and women before Allah ﷻ (33:35). The Prophet consulted Umm Salamah when the Companions were slow to carry out his instruction at Hudaybiyyah (Bukhari 2731-2732; verify). 'The best of you are the best to their wives' is reported in Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah and graded sahih; teacher to verify the number. Ask pupils: what does 'live with them in kindness' require in practice?

teach.heading: Rights given to women
bullets: Right to own wealth and receive inheritance (Qur'an 4:7)
Consent is needed for marriage (Bukhari 5136, Muslim 1419)
Right to seek knowledge and take part in society
Mahr belongs to the bride
teach.note: Present rights historically: before Islam many women could not inherit or choose. Say respectfully that Muslims and non-Muslims discuss how rights work in practice today and that cultures sometimes fall short of Islamic teaching; the spec asks what the Prophet ﷺ taught. Marriage consent hadith: verify numbers before quoting.

teach.heading: What does this show about society?
bullets: Family is the base of society
Respect is a religious duty
Women are partners in faith and community
Justice includes the home
teach.note: Ask pupils to move from evidence to belief: what does a society look like that applies these teachings? Note that this slide is a bridge to the evaluative 12-mark skill: use evidence, then draw a conclusion about Muslim belief.

teach.heading: Model answer (12 marks)
bullets: Claim
Evidence
Counter-view
Judgement
teach.note: Model a short plan.

model.problem: 'The Prophet's teachings show that Muslims believe women should be respected.' Assess this statement. (12 marks)
steps: For: he said mothers deserve the best company, three times over, and 33:35 gives women equal spiritual reward.
For: his example of consultation (Umm Salamah) and kindness at home shows respect in practice.
Counter-view: some cultures act differently, but Muslims say that is not the teaching.
Judgement: the sources strongly support respect; failures come from ignoring them, not from the teaching.
model.answer: Level 4: balanced, uses sources, reaches a supported conclusion.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Discuss why the other options fail.

check.q: In the hadith about the best companion, who is named first?
check.why: The mother is named three times before the father.

practice: Name one ayah about parents.
Give two rights women were given.
What does 'ihsan' mean?
independent: Core: create a two-column table of teachings and examples.
Extend: write a 6-mark answer on respect for mothers.
Stretch: plan a 12-mark essay on the statement above.
exit: State the hadith about mothers in your own words.
Give one example of the Prophet ﷺ consulting a woman.
Big question: what do these teachings show about Muslim society?
lessons.homework: Write a letter to a friend explaining why Islam teaches that mothers deserve great respect.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sentence frames for evidence-explain; stretch: compare examples of the Prophet's family life across sources.

lessons.unit: Spec 1.7: The Prophet as leader (Section A)
lessons.title: 1.7 The Prophet as leader: establishing the Shari'ah in Madinah
lessons.bigQuestion: How did the Prophet ﷺ build a lawful community in Madinah?
objectives: Define Shari'ah and ummah
Describe how the Prophet ﷺ established the Shari'ah after the Hijrah
Explain his role as judge, lawgiver and guide
successCriteria: All: define Shari'ah and give an example of a Madinan rule
Most: explain how the Prophet ﷺ established law and order in Madinah
Some: assess why Madinah was the turning point for Islamic law
lessons.crossCurricular: History: how leaders form states; Citizenship: law-making and justice
lessons.smsc: Social: community, justice and responsibility; Moral: following guidance from Allah ﷻ

keywords.def: the way or law that Allah has laid down

starter: Why did the Prophet ﷺ migrate to Madinah?
Name one thing the Prophet ﷺ built in Madinah.

teach.heading: From Makkah to Madinah
bullets: Makkah: belief in Allah ﷻ, patience, character
Madinah: community, law, trade, defence
The Prophet was guide and head of state
Revelation continued to give detailed rules
teach.note: Bismillah. Explain that Makkan revelation emphasised belief and good character; Madinan revelation included the detailed laws. Be careful: lots of worship was introduced earlier (prayer in Makkah). Use the idea of 'stages'.

teach.heading: Developing the Shari'ah
bullets: Qibla changed to the Ka'bah (Qur'an 2:142-150)
Fasting in Ramadan prescribed (Qur'an 2:183)
Zakah organised as a duty
Alcohol prohibited in stages (Qur'an 2:219, 4:43, 5:90-91)
teach.note: Teach the examples: change of qiblah in 2 AH; fasting also in 2 AH; zakah system; gradual prohibition of alcohol. Hajj became obligatory by a later point (scholars differ on the exact year; teacher can say 'by 9 or 10 AH'). Give the verses as support and ask pupils to check. Link to the Shari'ah being gradual and merciful.

teach.heading: Judge and leader
bullets: Qur'an 4:65: they do not believe until they accept your judgement
People brought disputes to him
He consulted his Companions (shura) in many matters
He made agreements and treaties
teach.note: 4:65 is secure; verify the wording. Ask: what does it mean for a leader to be judge as well as guide? Give an example of consulting on strategy (Badr, Uhud) which pupils know from Y11 lessons later. The Prophet is not a king: he is a Messenger, guided by revelation.

teach.heading: Model answer
bullets: Define
Give evidence
Explain significance
teach.note: Model an exam answer.

model.problem: Explain how the Prophet ﷺ established the Shari'ah in Madinah. (6 marks)
steps: Point: he received revelation giving detailed rules, for example fasting in Ramadan and the change of qiblah.
Explain: these gave the Muslims clear practices which unified the community.
Point: he acted as judge, settling disputes with justice.
Explain: this showed that the law applied to everyone and created order after years of tribal rivalry.
model.answer: Two developed points, linked to establishing law.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Reveal.

check.q: Which of these was prescribed in Madinah?
options: The change of qiblah to the Ka'bah
check.why: The qiblah changed to Makkah in Madinah. The other events were in Makkah.

practice: Define Shari'ah.
Name two rules developed in Madinah.
Why is the Prophet's role as judge important?
independent: Core: complete a table of Makkan and Madinan emphasis.
Extend: write a 6-mark answer on how the Shari'ah was established.
Stretch: argue why Madinah was the turning point for the development of Islamic law.
exit: Give one example of a ruling given in Madinah.
What is the ummah?
Big question: how did the Prophet ﷺ build a lawful community?

Describe the expansion through Hudaybiyyah, the conquest of Makkah and the delegations
Explain the importance of these events for Islam

the conquest of Makkah in 8 AH
the Negus: Christian king of Abyssinia

starter: Where did the Prophet's followers first emigrate for safety?
Which three battles do we study in Year 11?

bullets: Madinah consolidated (1-5 AH)
Hudaybiyyah 6 AH
Conquest of Makkah 8 AH
Year of Delegations 9 AH
teach.note: Let pupils place events. Dates: Hijrah 1 AH (622 CE); Badr 2 AH; Uhud 3; Trench 5; Hudaybiyyah 6; Khaybar 7; conquest 8; Tabuk and delegations 9; Farewell Hajj 10 AH; death 11 AH. Teachers should confirm dates with a trusted Sira text, as some scholars differ slightly.

timeline.label: 1 AH
timeline.text: Hijrah; mosque and pact in Madinah

teach.heading: Hudaybiyyah
bullets: Muslims set out for umrah; Quraysh blocked them
Terms: truce for ten years; return the following year
Many Companions found the terms hard
Qur'an called it a clear victory (Qur'an 48:1)
teach.note: The treaty looked unfavourable on the surface; Umar and others were troubled, but the truce allowed da'wah and growth. 48:1 is secure; verify the wording. Ask: how can a pause in fighting help a community? Emphasise trust in the Prophet's leadership.

teach.heading: The conquest of Makkah
bullets: Quraysh's ally broke the truce
The Prophet marched with a large army
Makkah entered with almost no fighting
He declared general amnesty and cleansed the Ka'bah of idols
teach.note: Teach the well-known facts: ten thousand marched; near-bloodless; the idols were removed from the Ka'bah. The Prophet's address to Quraysh promising 'Go, you are free' is widely reported in Sira sources; no hadith number is given here and teacher to verify before quoting. Ask: what does his treatment of people who had persecuted him for years show about his leadership?

teach.heading: Delegations and expansion
bullets: Tribes from across Arabia sent delegations
Letters were sent to rulers inviting to Islam
Tabuk expedition 9 AH to meet the threat from the north
By his death most of Arabia was united
teach.note: Note the sensitivity: expansion was political and religious; pupils should know both. Present sources: Hudaybiyyah, conquest, delegations are well documented. Ask: why did tribes come after Makkah opened? (Quraysh was the leading tribe.)

teach.heading: Model answer
bullets: Cause
Event
Effect
teach.note: Model a 6-mark answer.

model.problem: Explain why the conquest of Makkah was important for Islam. (6 marks)
steps: Point: it removed the centre of opposition and gave Muslims control of the Haram.
Explain: with Quraysh no longer hostile, other tribes felt free to join.
Point: the Prophet's forgiveness showed Islam's character in victory.
Explain: this turned former enemies into supporters and set a model for later Muslim rulers.
model.answer: Developed reasoning shown in both strands: political and moral.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Reveal.

check.q: What was the main effect of the treaty of Hudaybiyyah?
options: It created a ten-year truce which allowed peaceful growth
It made the Prophet leave Arabia
check.why: The truce allowed contact, da'wah and growth. The other options are false.

practice: Put Hudaybiyyah, conquest of Makkah and Tabuk in order.
What did the Prophet ﷺ do at the Ka'bah in Makkah?
Why was Hudaybiyyah called a clear victory?
independent: Core: complete a cause-and-effect chart for the conquest.
Extend: write a 6-mark answer on why Makkah was important.
Stretch: compare Hudaybiyyah and the conquest as two forms of success.
exit: Give one result of the conquest.
Define wufud.
Big question: how did Islam become secure?
lessons.homework: Write a news report from Makkah on the day of the conquest, with accuracy and mercy.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: map of Arabia with key places; stretch: evaluate sources on the conquest.

lessons.unit: Spec 1.7: The Prophet as leader (Section A)
lessons.title: 1.7 Opponents, prisoners and relations with other communities and countries (hadith on obedience to rulers)
lessons.bigQuestion: How did the Prophet ﷺ treat his enemies and deal with other nations, and why should Muslims obey a leader?
objectives: Describe his treatment of opponents and prisoners
Describe his relations with other communities and states
Analyse the hadith on obedience to rulers and its limits
successCriteria: All: give two examples of how he treated prisoners or enemies
Most: explain his diplomacy with other rulers
Some: assess the limits of obedience to leaders in the hadith, with evidence
lessons.crossCurricular: Citizenship: rule of law, rights of prisoners; History: diplomacy
lessons.smsc: Moral: mercy and justice; Social: responsibilities of citizens and rulers

keywords.def: a person under a treaty of peace

starter: What happened at Makkah in 8 AH?

teach.heading: Treatment of prisoners
bullets: Badr prisoners were housed and treated kindly
Some literate prisoners earned freedom by teaching Muslim children
Thumamah ibn Uthal was held in the mosque, then freed and accepted Islam (Bukhari 462)
Qur'an 76:8: feeding the captive
teach.note: Badr prisoners: ransom or teaching reading and writing is well known in Sira; verify before quoting. The Thumamah story is in Bukhari (verify number). 76:8 'they feed, for love of Allah ﷻ, the poor, the orphan and the captive' is secure. Ask: what does this show about treatment of prisoners? Link to the Geneva Convention only as modern parallel for pupils' interest, not as a claim.

teach.heading: Opponents
bullets: Mercy at Makkah: amnesty for Quraysh
Hypocrites in Madinah were not executed for their lack of faith
Some tribes that broke treaties faced consequences
Banu Qurayzah: arbitration after betrayal during the Trench
teach.note: SENSITIVE: teach accurately and calmly. Banu Qurayzah broke their agreement during the siege (Trench, 5 AH); the judgement was given by Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, their chosen arbiter, according to their own law (Torah) as many Sira sources state; scholars discuss the sources. Present as a political and military matter of treason, not a religious judgement on Jews, and reject any use of the event to justify hatred. Teachers should pre-read and keep this factual. For safeguarding, invite questions but do not allow stereotyping. Mention that other Jewish tribes were exiled after breaking the pact, rather than killed.

teach.heading: Relations with other countries
bullets: Letters invited rulers to Islam: Heraclius, Negus, Khosrau
Heraclius's reply was respectful (Bukhari 7)
The Negus gave refuge to the early Muslims
Envoys were treated with respect
teach.note: Bukhari 7 is the narration of the letter to Heraclius and Abu Sufyan's replies (verify). Keep to the secure points: letters were sent; the Negus protected the emigrants; diplomacy was used. Ask: why use letters rather than force? (Da'wah and diplomacy.)

teach.heading: Obedience to rulers
bullets: Qur'an 4:59: obey Allah ﷻ, the Messenger and those in authority
Hadith: obey your leader in what is good
No obedience in what is sinful (Bukhari 7257, Muslim 1840)
The ruler is also accountable: each is a shepherd (Bukhari 893, Muslim 1829)
teach.note: The spec passage is a hadith on obedience to rulers, printed in Appendix 5. Teacher should read the printed hadith and annotate with pupils. Two secure principles: obedience in what is good only, and accountability of leaders. Verify the numbers. Frame for British context: Muslims obey the law of the land they live in as part of their covenant of security; obedience never includes sin; and extremist violence is never justified by this hadith. Flag for safeguarding.

teach.heading: Model answer
bullets: Plan
Evidence
Evaluate
teach.note: Model a 12-mark approach.

model.problem: 'Muslims must always obey their rulers.' Assess this statement. (12 marks)
steps: For: Qur'an 4:59 commands obedience to those in authority, and the hadith stresses hearing and obeying.
For: order and unity are valued; the Prophet ﷺ established leadership.
Against: obedience is in what is good only (Bukhari 7257, Muslim 1840), so no obedience in sin.
Judgement: Muslims should obey just authority within limits; this is neither blind obedience nor rebellion.
model.answer: Level 4: clear for/against with specific sources and a reasoned conclusion.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Reveal.

check.q: What limit does the hadith set on obedience to a ruler?
options: Obedience is only in what is good
check.why: Obedience is in what is good; there is none in disobedience of Allah ﷻ.

practice: Give two examples of mercy to prisoners.
Name two rulers who received letters.
What does Qur'an 4:59 command?
independent: Core: summarise the hadith in two sentences and underline its limit.
Extend: write a 6-mark answer on the Prophet's treatment of prisoners.
Stretch: plan the 12-mark answer above.
exit: Define fidyah.
State the limit on obedience.
Big question: how should leaders and followers behave?
lessons.homework: Revise Section A: choose one of the Section A units we have learned and write five key facts.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: annotated hadith with glossary; stretch: compare the roles of obedience and accountability.

lessons.title: 3.1 The Shahadah: nature, role and use in Muslim life (Qur'an 3:18-19)
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is a single sentence the foundation of a Muslim's faith?
objectives: State the Shahadah in Arabic and English and explain its two parts
Explain the importance of reciting the Shahadah
Describe how the Shahadah is used in practice, from birth to death
successCriteria: All: recite and translate the Shahadah
Most: explain what each part commits a Muslim to
Some: evaluate whether saying the Shahadah is enough to be a Muslim
lessons.crossCurricular: Arabic: reading and translating the kalimah; PSHE: identity and belonging
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: sincerity of belief; Cultural: how a single declaration unites a diverse ummah

keywords.def: the declaration of faith: the first pillar

keywords.term: la ilaha illa Allah (لا إله إلا الله)
keywords.def: there is no god but Allah
Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah

starter: Name the five pillars in order.
Which pillar do the others depend on?
What is the meaning of Tawhid?

teach.heading: The words and meaning
bullets: أشهد أن لا إله إلا الله وأشهد أن محمدا رسول الله
I bear witness that there is no god but Allah ﷻ
and I bear witness that Muhammad ﷺ is the Messenger of Allah ﷻ
Part one: Tawhid. Part two: Risalah
teach.note: Bismillah. Have pupils say the Shahadah aloud together. Break it into negation (no god) and affirmation (but Allah ﷻ). Link to Tawhid in Year 11 unit 2.1 and risalah. Explain that a Muslim's testimony includes belief in the heart, speech by tongue and action by limbs; scholars give conditions of the Shahadah, which can be taught as understanding, sincerity and acceptance. Verify the Arabic script in the mushaf before display.

teach.heading: Qur'an 3:18-19
bullets: Allah ﷻ bears witness that there is no god but Him
The angels and people of knowledge also bear witness
He upholds justice
The true religion with Allah ﷻ is Islam (submission)
teach.note: This is the set passage. 3:18: شَهِدَ اللَّهُ أَنَّهُ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ... 3:19: إِنَّ الدِّينَ عِندَ اللَّهِ الْإِسْلَامُ. Teacher to check the wording from the mushaf and a trusted translation. Note: 'Islam' here means submission to Allah ﷻ; scholars explain it as the way of all prophets. Do not push exclusivist readings; present the text and how Muslims understand it. Ask: who is a witness in this ayah? Why is Allah's own testimony powerful?

teach.heading: Importance of reciting it
bullets: Entry into Islam: said sincerely with understanding
The first thing whispered to a newborn (adhan)
Repeated in the call to prayer and in every prayer
Said at the end of life when possible
teach.note: Describe how the Shahadah is used: conversion (said before witnesses, no minimum ritual beyond sincerity), adhan and iqamah, tashahhud in salah, and the encouragement to say it at the end of life (verify any hadith number before quoting; do not quote 'whoever's last words' without checking its grading). Hadith of Mu'adh: Prophet told him to call people first to the Shahadah (Bukhari 1395, Muslim 19; verify). Ask pupils which of these they hear in daily life.

head: Occasion
How the Shahadah appears
rows: Declared with sincerity, ideally before witnesses

teach.heading: Model answer
bullets: Meaning
Role
Importance
teach.note: Model an exam answer.

model.problem: Explain why the Shahadah is the most important pillar. (6 marks)
steps: Point: it expresses Tawhid, the core belief of Islam, that only Allah ﷻ is worshipped.
Explain: without it the other pillars have no foundation.
Point: it also affirms Muhammad ﷺ as Messenger, so Muslims follow his Sunnah.
Explain: this guides how every act of worship is performed, and it unites Muslims of all backgrounds.
model.answer: Two developed points; keeps the focus on 'why most important'.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Reveal.

check.q: Which belief does the first half of the Shahadah express?
check.why: The first half affirms the oneness of Allah ﷻ. The second half affirms the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ (risalah).

practice: Say the Shahadah in Arabic and translate.
Identify two occasions where the Shahadah is spoken.
What does 3:18 say about who bears witness?
independent: Core: complete a diagram linking the two halves to Tawhid and Risalah.
Extend: write a 6-mark answer on the importance of the Shahadah.
Stretch: write 8 lines responding to 'Saying the Shahadah is enough to be a Muslim' with scholarly views noted.
exit: State the Shahadah in English.
Give one place the Shahadah appears in salah.
Big question: why does one sentence found a Muslim's faith?
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph for a non-Muslim friend explaining what the Shahadah means and how Muslims use it.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: audio of the Shahadah, transliteration and picture cards; stretch: explore conditions of the Shahadah and how scholars differ on its minimum requirements.

lessons.title: 3.2 Salah: nature, significance and importance
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do Muslims stop what they are doing five times a day?
objectives: Describe the nature and purpose of Salah
Explain its significance and importance in Muslim life
Link to the Qur'an and Sunnah
successCriteria: All: name the five daily prayers and when they occur
Most: explain three reasons Salah matters
Some: evaluate the claim that Salah is the most important pillar after the Shahadah
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: routine, wellbeing and mindfulness; Geography: times of prayer through the year
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: connection with Allah ﷻ; Social: community and discipline
starter: How many rak'ahs are in Fajr?
What is the direction of prayer?

teach.heading: What Salah is
bullets: The second pillar of Islam
Five prescribed prayers each day
A direct link between the servant and Allah ﷻ
Fixed times: Qur'an 4:103
teach.note: Bismillah. Mention that the five prayers were prescribed at the Mi'raj (a link back to Unit 1.4). Hadith: 'Islam is built on five' (Bukhari 8, Muslim 16; verify). Qur'an 4:103: prayer is prescribed for believers at fixed times (secure; check mushaf). Ask pupils what they know of the daily structure of prayers.

teach.heading: Why it matters
bullets: Reminds Muslims of Allah ﷻ during the day
Teaches discipline and equality: all stand in lines
Cleanses the heart and prevents wrongdoing (Qur'an 29:45)
Five prayers are like a river at the door, washing away dirt (Muslim 668)
teach.note: 29:45 'prayer prevents immorality and wrongdoing' secure; the river hadith is in Muslim 668 (verify wording). Ask: how might repeated prayer shape a person? Compare to athletic training. The hadith that abandoning prayer is the difference between a person and disbelief (Muslim 82) is a serious warning and scholars differ on its meaning; teacher to handle with care and avoid frightening pupils.

teach.heading: Salah in numbers
bullets: Fajr 2 rak'ahs, Dhuhr 4, 'Asr 4
Maghrib 3, 'Isha' 4 (fard)
Extra prayers: sunnah and nafl
Jummah replaces Dhuhr on Friday
teach.note: Give pupils the numbers as a table to memorise. Note that Hanafi and other schools differ over classifications such as wajib for witr; the spec asks for the main pattern. Keep neutral.

teach.heading: Model answer
bullets: Point
Evidence
Explain
teach.note: Model a 6-mark answer.

model.problem: Explain why Salah is important for Muslims. (6 marks)
steps: Point: it is a pillar of Islam, so Muslims must perform it.
Evidence: the Qur'an says prayer is prescribed at fixed times (4:103).
Explain: regular prayer keeps a Muslim conscious of Allah ﷻ throughout the day.
Point: congregational prayer builds unity.
Explain: when Muslims stand shoulder to shoulder, differences in wealth or race are set aside.
model.answer: Two reasons, each developed with Islamic evidence.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Reveal.

check.q: How many fard rak'ahs are there in Maghrib?
check.why: Maghrib has three. Fajr has two; Dhuhr, Asr and Isha have four.

practice: List the five prayers in order.
Give two benefits of Salah.
Which ayah says prayer prevents wrongdoing?
independent: Core: fill the table of five prayers and rak'ahs.
Extend: write a 6-mark answer on the importance of Salah.
Stretch: write a short reflection on how daily prayer could shape discipline in your own life.
exit: Name the prayer with three rak'ahs.
Give one Qur'an reference on prayer.
Big question: why do Muslims stop five times a day?
lessons.homework: Interview a family member or friend about their experience of Salah and write a short summary.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: visual timeline of the day with prayer times; stretch: investigate how prayer times are calculated in the UK across the year.

lessons.title: 3.2 How Salah is performed: wudu, times, qiblah, movements and recitations
lessons.bigQuestion: What does a Muslim do, step by step, when praying?
objectives: Describe wudu and when it is needed
Describe the times, direction, movements and recitations of Salah
Explain the meaning behind the main parts
successCriteria: All: put the stages of salah in order
Most: describe wudu and qiblah accurately
Some: explain the meaning of key recitations and postures
lessons.crossCurricular: Arabic: reading the key phrases; PE: posture and movement
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: humility; Moral: cleanliness and discipline

teach.heading: Wudu and purity
bullets: Wash hands, mouth and nose
Face, arms to the elbows
Wipe the head, wash ears and feet
Qur'an 5:6; ghusl and tayammum when needed
teach.note: Qur'an 5:6 describes wudu: face, arms to the elbows, wiping the head, feet. Many scholars add the details of hands, mouth and nose from the Sunnah. Mention tayammum when no water. Schools differ on what breaks wudu; here give the common points (using the toilet, sleep, passing wind). Neutral note: Shia wudu involves wiping the feet instead of washing, based on their reading of 5:6; present without ranking.

teach.heading: Times and direction
bullets: Prayer times are set by the sun
Face the Ka'bah in Makkah (Qur'an 2:144)
The qiblah unites Muslims worldwide
Travel and missed prayers have concessions
teach.note: 2:144 'turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque' secure; check wording. Note: the Prophet ﷺ first faced Jerusalem before the change in Madinah. For missed prayers: Bukhari 597 (pray when remembered; verify). For travel: shortening is allowed (4:101); neutral on duration since schools differ.

teach.heading: The movements and words
bullets: Takbir 'Allahu akbar' (الله أكبر)
Standing: recite al-Fatihah and a short surah
Ruku', then standing, then two sujud with a sitting between
Tashahhud and salam: السلام عليكم ورحمة الله
teach.note: Be careful to describe the common core. Words: Subhana Rabbiyal 'Adhim in ruku'; Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah; Subhana Rabbiyal A'la in sujud. A rak'ah is one cycle. Note that some schools place the hands differently and some say 'amin' aloud (and Shia Muslims may keep arms at the sides or use a clay tablet for the forehead); teach neutrally as 'differences of practice' and avoid ranking. Hadith: 'Pray as you have seen me pray' (Bukhari 631; verify).

teach.heading: Model answer
bullets: Order
Detail
Meaning
teach.note: Model a 'describe' answer.

model.problem: Describe how a Muslim performs one rak'ah of Salah. (4 marks)
steps: Stands facing qiblah, says 'Allahu akbar', and recites al-Fatihah and a short surah.
Bows in ruku', saying words of glorification.
Stands up, then goes into sujud, forehead on the ground.
Sits briefly, performs a second sujud, and rises.
model.answer: Four accurate, ordered stages with correct terms.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Reveal.

options: Prostration with the forehead on the ground
check.why: Sujud is prostration. Ruku' is bowing; qiyam is standing; tashahhud is the sitting testimony.

practice: Put the steps of wudu in order.
What does 'Allahu akbar' mean?
Name two reasons a Muslim performs wudu.
independent: Core: label the postures of a rak'ah.
Extend: write a 4-mark answer describing one rak'ah.
Stretch: explain the meaning behind sujud as the closest a servant is to Allah ﷻ (teacher supplies the verified hadith).
exit: What is the qiblah?
Name the posture of bowing.
Big question: what does a Muslim do, step by step, when praying?
lessons.homework: Learn the Arabic words for four postures and write what each means.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: picture sequence with transliteration; stretch: compare practices of prayer across schools of thought.

lessons.title: 3.2 Salah in the home, the mosque and Jummah (Qur'an 62:9-11); exemptions
lessons.bigQuestion: Where and when do Muslims pray, and who is excused?
objectives: Compare prayer at home, in the mosque and at Friday prayer
Analyse Qur'an 62:9-11
Describe exemptions and concessions in Salah
successCriteria: All: say what is special about Jummah
Most: explain the value of congregational prayer
Some: evaluate how far exemptions show the flexibility of Islam
lessons.crossCurricular: Citizenship: religious practice in a multi-faith society; Geography: mosques and communities
lessons.smsc: Social: community cohesion; Moral: balance of worship and work

teach.heading: Home or mosque?
bullets: Prayer may be offered at home alone
Prayer in congregation carries extra reward (Bukhari 645, Muslim 650)
The mosque is a centre for learning and community
Men are strongly encouraged to attend; women may pray at home or at the mosque
teach.note: The reward of congregation (27 degrees) is reported in Bukhari 645 and Muslim 650; verify. Note differences: many scholars regard congregation as obligatory for men and others as strongly recommended; Hanafis and others differ on women. Present neutrally. In Britain many mosques provide space for women. Ask: what are the benefits of praying together?

teach.heading: Qur'an 62:9-11
bullets: When called to Friday prayer, hasten to the remembrance of Allah ﷻ
Leave off business
After the prayer, disperse and seek Allah's bounty
Do not abandon the khutbah for trade or amusement
teach.note: 62:9 يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِذَا نُودِيَ لِلصَّلَاةِ مِن يَوْمِ الْجُمُعَةِ فَاسْعَوْا إِلَىٰ ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ وَذَرُوا الْبَيْعَ. Teacher to verify the Arabic. 62:11 speaks of people leaving the Prophet ﷺ standing in the khutbah when a caravan arrived. Ask: what balance between work and worship does the passage give? (Stop for the prayer, then return to work.)

teach.heading: Jummah
bullets: Two parts: khutbah then two rak'ahs
Held at midday on Friday, replacing Dhuhr
Obligatory for adult men; women may attend
Teaches the community, gives reminders and unity
teach.note: Describe the day: ghusl, clean clothes, early arrival, khutbah in two parts, two rak'ahs led by the imam. Mention that British workplaces and schools may accommodate Jummah; many pupils will have experience. Exemptions: women, travellers, sick people, children (not required).

teach.heading: Exemptions and concessions
bullets: Sick: pray sitting or lying (Bukhari 1117)
Travellers may shorten and combine (4:101)
Menstruation and postnatal bleeding: no prayer and no make-up
Children below puberty and those who lose capacity are not obliged
teach.note: Bukhari 1117: pray standing, if not able sit, if not able on your side (verify). Women's exemption is well known; note that prayer missed during menses is not made up (Aisha's report; verify). Safeguarding: be matter-of-fact and age-appropriate; invite questions privately. Combining prayers: Hanafi and Shia approaches differ from others; teach the concession neutrally.

teach.heading: Model answer
bullets: Evidence
Evaluate
Judgement
teach.note: Model a 12-mark plan.

model.problem: 'The benefits of Hajj are greater than the challenges.' Assess this statement. (12 marks)
steps: For: pilgrims gain forgiveness, unity and a lifetime memory of equality.
For: challenges such as heat and cost are limited to once in a lifetime and are accepted as service to Allah ﷻ.
Against: for some, cost, illness or crowds are serious barriers.
Judgement: benefits outweigh challenges for most, and Islam adjusts the duty for those unable.
